masthead_title: The whole Treasury curve confirms the hawkish turn, while a wildfire-liability bill craters California utilities
regime_line: Every Treasury tenor this system tracks — 3-month, 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year — is flagged together for the first time this cycle, confirming Friday's hawkish Fed repricing held through Monday's close and formally resolving an open claim, even as a separate, far larger single-day shock — a failed California wildfire-liability bill — cut two utility giants by a fifth to a quarter of their value overnight.
provenance_note: Stated reasons and press framing via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): Bloomberg, Benzinga, Forbes, 24/7 Wall St., MoneyCheck, The Motley Fool, CNBC, NBC News, BusinessToday, TipRanks. No paid services used.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one confirmed, two still open, one new

Yesterday's brief left three claims live. One grades cleanly today; the other two are updated below before any new narrative is written (§4B).

  • CL-0006 — confirmed. Opened Friday: does Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech hold, tested by whether the 2-year Treasury yield rose 4 basis points or more from Friday's pre-speech close of 4.20%, by Monday 08-31's close. Monday's actual close is now in this system's data: the 2-year finished at 4.34% — unchanged from Friday's post-speech level, but still +14 basis points versus the 4.20% baseline, more than triple the +4bp bar. Confirmed.
  • CL-0005 — still open (due 2026-09-02, one trading day left). Semis (SMH) added 0.63% Monday against the S&P 500's 0.30% decline, pulling the cumulative read since the 08-25 baseline back to essentially flat (−0.0 percentage points, script-computed from macro_series.csv) — a real recovery from Friday's −0.94pp reading, and comfortably inside the −2pp floor that would refute the claim.
  • CL-0007 — still open (due 2026-09-03, grading against that specific day's close, not a running average). Directionally supportive so far: this system's own WTI series closed Monday at $85.76 (+2.83% on the day), already above the $85 line the claim will test, two trading days ahead of schedule.

A new conditional claim opened this morning: CL-0008 — Monday's California wildfire-liability selloff in Edison International and PG&E (see Movers, below) is a state-specific regulatory shock, not an early sign of stress bleeding into broader utility or investment-grade credit, tested by whether this system's own IG OAS series stays at or below 0.84% (no more than +5bp from Friday's 0.79% base) through 2026-09-09.
story_html:
This morning's press narrative runs on three tracks. First, Fed policy: coverage (CNBC, Bloomberg) leads with fed funds futures now pricing roughly 60-66% odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 15-16 meeting, up sharply since Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech Friday — though CNBC also notes "not everyone is convinced," with some desks (Goldman Sachs, per that same coverage) pushing back on how hawkish a read this really is. Second, oil and Iran: overnight and this morning, President Trump said Iran was "totally defeated militarily" while threatening further strikes, and Brent crude touched $91.52 intraday (NBC News, BusinessToday) — a fresh escalation on top of the weekend's initial U.S. strike near the Strait of Hormuz. Third, and by far the largest single-day dollar move: a failed California wildfire-liability bill sent Edison International and PG&E to their worst trading days in decades (Bloomberg, Benzinga, Forbes) — a state-specific regulatory story, covered in full in Movers below rather than folded into the macro narrative here.

Does the state file confirm the Fed story? Cleanly, and for the first time this cycle, across the whole curve. The 3-month, 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year Treasury yields are all flagged simultaneously today (z +1.58 to +1.81 — higher than all but a handful of days in the past six months), and the 2-year — the market's clearest live poll of near-term Fed expectations — held exactly flat at Friday's post-speech close of 4.34%, which is itself the data point that formally confirms CL-0006 today (see Claims, above). Gold, which tends to fall when the market prices a tighter Fed and higher real interest rates, slipped a further 1.06% to $4,431.10, a second confirmation in the same direction. The oil story the data can partially confirm: this system's own WTI series closed Monday at $85.76, up 2.83% on the day and already past the $85 line CL-0007 will test on 2026-09-03 — though this morning's further escalation (Trump's comments, Brent above $91) isn't in this system's data yet and is reported here as attributed context, not a verified fact. Equities took both the rate story and the utility shock in stride: the S&P 500 slipped a modest 0.33% to 7,686.14 (1.45% off its all-time closing high), and credit didn't confirm any broad stress — high-yield spreads (dated Friday, one-day lag) sit near a six-month low (z −1.28).
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-08-31 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, both credit-spread series, and SOFR publish a day behind (§5), dated to Friday 08-28; Fed balance sheet and TGA are the weekly Thursday H.4.1 release, dated to Wednesday 08-26. Flagged rows (⚑): far outside the past-6-months normal range — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: Monday's Treasury session was quiet in its own right — the 2-year didn't move at all (4.34%, unchanged), and the 10-year and 30-year each added just 2-3 basis points — but because Friday's hawkish repricing pushed the whole curve to levels this system hasn't seen since it started keeping score, all four tenors (3-month, 2-year, 10-year, 30-year) are now flagged together for the first time this cycle (z +1.58 to +1.81). That matters in real terms for anyone with an adjustable-rate loan, a money-market fund, or a CD coming due for renewal: the market isn't pricing a one-day scare, it's sitting at genuinely elevated levels across the whole maturity spectrum. Using Friday's fully-published data (the most recent day with every piece available, one day behind Monday's close): the 10-year's 6bp rise broke down almost perfectly into its two components — the real yield (what investors demand after inflation, mostly a growth-and-Fed-policy number) rose 8bp, from 2.34% to 2.42%, while the breakeven (the market's implied inflation rate) actually fell 2bp, from 2.33% to 2.31%. Add those together (+8bp and −2bp) and you get +6bp, matching the nominal move to the basis point — today's concept segment walks through exactly why that arithmetic matters. Credit stayed unbothered: high-yield spreads (2.60%, dated Friday) sit near a six-month low (z −1.28) and investment-grade spreads are flat at 0.79% — a genuine, quiet positive that argues this is a rates story, not a growth or credit-quality scare. One technical note: the overnight reverse repo facility (where money-market funds park spare cash overnight) jumped from $0.18B to $6.73B — a large-looking move (z +1.05) — but Monday was the last trading day of August, and RRP balances reliably spike at month-end as funds temporarily can't find better short-term lending options; read here as calendar plumbing, not a liquidity signal. Fed balance sheet and Treasury cash balance remain "thin history" series (§4) — directional only, no z-score confidence yet.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 39 name candidates and 3 sector divergences qualified Monday; cap is 3 names + a sector note. "Stated reason" is what reporting said, not necessarily what's true.

EIX −26.74% (53.98, from 73.68) — what happened: Edison International's worst trading day since the 2001 California energy crisis. Stated reason: a wildfire-liability bill introduced in Sacramento over the weekend left investor-owned utilities on the hook for fire-related claims after lawmakers rejected a plan to strip insurers of subrogation rights; Mizuho downgraded the stock to neutral and cut its price target to $70 (Bloomberg, Benzinga, 24/7 Wall St.). Why it matters: a state-specific regulatory and legal shock, not a broad macro signal — nothing in today's credit data shows contagion yet — but large enough in single-day dollar terms to dwarf an entire flagged Treasury curve, and big enough that this brief is logging a new claim (CL-0008, above) to check whether it stays contained to these two names or spreads into utility-sector or investment-grade credit more broadly.

PCG −20.06% (13.27, from 16.60) — what happened: PG&E's sharpest one-day decline since emerging from its 2019 wildfire bankruptcy, in the same selloff as Edison International above. Stated reason: the company said the weekend's wildfire-liability legislation "does not adequately address the financing risks" in California's wildfire framework and lacks the "long-term durability" to attract investment; BMO Capital cut the stock to Market Perform and raised its estimated wildfire-liability drag to $10 a share from $6 (Forbes, MoneyCheck). Why it matters: the same read-through as Edison above — tracked jointly under CL-0008 rather than as two separate stories.

SLB +9.25% (60.10, from 55.01) — what happened: Schlumberger's largest S&P gain Monday, alongside broad gains for Exxon Mobil and Chevron. Stated reason: energy stocks rallied with oil prices, which climbed on the weekend's U.S. strike on Iranian rocket launchers near the Strait of Hormuz (The Motley Fool). Why it matters: the cleanest macro read-through among today's movers — SLB is a levered proxy for the same oil-risk-premium story behind the open CL-0007 claim, and a 9%+ move shows that risk premium is already being priced into equities, not just crude futures.

Sector note: Energy (XLE) beat the S&P 500 by 2.34 percentage points Monday (+2.04% vs. −0.30%), the largest of three sector divergences that cleared this system's mechanical 1.5pp threshold — Utilities (−1.90pp) and Industrials (−1.75pp) also qualified, both consistent with the wildfire-liability selloff above dragging on rate-sensitive and industrial-adjacent names; no separate, clearly-attributed catalyst surfaced for Industrials specifically, so that one is reported as a fact worth watching, not a story this brief can explain yet. Energy's sector-wide breadth confirms SLB's move above wasn't a single-stock story.
chart_of_day_why: The largest |z| flag on the entire board today is the 10-year Treasury yield (z +1.81, edging out the 30-year's +1.80 and the 2-year's +1.66) — the whole curve is flagged together for the first time this cycle, and the 10-year is the single largest of the four by a hair. The 2-year is arguably the more direct read on near-term Fed expectations (and is what CL-0006 was built to grade, confirmed today), but the mechanical rule picks the single largest flag, and today that's the 10-year.

Financing watch: no new dated news on hyperscaler issuance or vendor-financing structures surfaced in this morning's search. Background reporting (not new today, cited for context) continues to describe rising spreads on hyperscaler bonds — J.P. Morgan Asset Management put median 2-4 year hyperscaler spreads at roughly 40 basis points over Treasurys, up from 30bp in 2025 — a mechanism worth remembering with long-end Treasury yields sitting at cycle highs today, but not a today-dated data point, so it isn't treated as new evidence.
calendar_note_html: Today's headline release is ISM Manufacturing PMI at 10:00am ET (forecast 55.2, previous 55.6, high impact) — worth watching precisely because of this morning's Fed story: a print at or above consensus would reinforce the picture of resilient growth backing a hawkish Fed, while a miss would complicate that narrative heading into a week that also brings ADP private payrolls and the Beige Book (Wednesday) and, Friday, the month's headline event — August nonfarm payrolls. JOLTS job openings lands at the same 10:00am ET slot (forecast 7.33M, previous 7.36M, medium impact) and speaks to the other side of the Fed's dual mandate: labor-market slack. Nothing today is a CPI- or FOMC-scale event on its own, but both releases feed directly into how confidently markets can keep pricing a September hike.
concept_unit: Unit 2 · Real vs. nominal decomposition · segment 2 of roughly 6
concept_title: Reading which piece moved: Friday's hawkish repricing, decomposed
concept_html: Yesterday's segment established the identity: nominal 10-year yield ≈ real yield (measured by TIPS, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) + breakeven inflation (the market's implied average inflation rate). Today, put it to work on an actual event. Friday's hawkish Jackson Hole speech pushed the nominal 10-year yield up 6 basis points, from 4.67% Thursday to 4.73% Friday (the most recent day with both pieces published). Split it: the real yield — roughly what investors demand to lend for ten years after inflation, mostly a growth-and-Fed-policy number — rose 8 basis points, from 2.34% to 2.42%. The breakeven — the market's implied inflation rate — actually fell 2 basis points, from 2.33% to 2.31%. Add the two moves together (+8bp and −2bp) and you get +6bp, matching the nominal move to the basis point. That's the tell: Friday's yield spike was almost entirely a real-yield story, not an inflation story. In plain terms, the market didn't get more worried about inflation coming back — it got more convinced the Fed will keep policy tight for longer, which is exactly what a hawkish speech should produce. A move driven by breakevens instead would point to a very different, inflation-scare narrative, with different implications for TIPS, commodities, and long-duration bonds.
client_translation: "When yields jump the way they did Friday, the first question I ask is whether it's the inflation piece or the real, after-inflation piece that moved — Friday it was almost entirely the real piece, which tells us this was a 'the Fed is staying tougher for longer' move, not a fresh inflation scare."
client_lens_html:
• "Did you see what happened to Edison and PG&E?" — Two of the largest utility-stock declines in decades, both on the same California wildfire-liability news (see Movers, above), not on anything company-specific like earnings. Useful illustration that a single state's legislative outcome can move a stock more in one day than an entire flagged Treasury curve moves in a week.
  • "Is the Fed actually going to raise rates in September?" — The data says the market thinks so, and increasingly: the 2-year Treasury yield (the clearest live poll of Fed expectations) confirmed Friday's hawkish move by holding at 4.34% through Monday, formally resolving a claim this brief logged Friday (CL-0006) rather than waiting to see. That's a real, data-confirmed shift in expectations — not a decision the Fed has made.
  • "Why is oil / gas expensive again?" — Reporting this morning describes President Trump threatening further strikes on Iran after the weekend's initial escalation near the Strait of Hormuz, with oil prices moving higher again. This system's own data confirms Monday's move (WTI +2.83% to $85.76) but doesn't yet have this morning's further escalation — that's exactly the kind of headline this brief waits to test rather than repeats on faith.
